overview.title: How This Course Works
overview.subtitle: Fifteen weeks from general security concepts to a passing score
body: Security+ is broader than a single-product exam. It's multiple-choice and performance-based, and it spans five domains that range from pure governance and risk theory to hands-on technical controls — firewalls, PKI, SIEM tooling, incident response. That breadth is exactly why this course runs longer than its RHCSA and LFCS siblings.

So this course is built around doing, not just memorizing acronyms. Every week has a focus, a short list of tasks, and a full lab guide — real tools, run on your own isolated lab VMs, never against a system you don't own. Where a topic is genuinely conceptual (governance frameworks, risk registers, compliance obligations), the guide says so and treats it as reading, not a fake lab.

This is CompTIA Security+, exam SY0-801 V8, built directly from CompTIA's official Exam Objectives document (version 1.4). At the time this course was written, CompTIA's own objectives document listed the exact question count and test length as "TBD" — SY0-801 had not fully launched. Everything else in this course — the five domains, their weightings, and every sub-objective — comes straight from that document. Check CompTIA's page before you book, in case the final logistics have since been published.

rhythm.text: hands-on labs on VMs you can break and rebuild — firewalls, certificates, logs, permissions, scans
reading and scenario practice — governance, risk, compliance, and incident-response processes
review — write down every term and acronym that didn't stick the first time

note.title: This exam has real, tested performance-based tasks
note.text: CompTIA lists the question format as multiple-choice and performance-based. That means some questions drop you into a simulated environment and ask you to actually configure something — not just recognize the right answer. Typing every command in this course's labs yourself, instead of reading past them, is not optional preparation. It's the actual exam format.

exam.title: What CompTIA Security+ V8 SY0-801 Actually Is
exam.subtitle: Format, domains, and what CompTIA is actually checking for
body: Security+ certifies that you can do five things: identify and support incident response activities, assess an environment's security posture and recommend fixes, manage and monitor modern environments including cloud/mobile/hybrid, operate with awareness of applicable regulations and governance, and apply mitigation techniques against threats and vulnerabilities. CompTIA's stated target audience is a security administrator with two years of hands-on experience — this course assumes less, and builds toward that bar.

domains.title: The five exam domains
rows: 1.0 General Security Concepts
Security controls, change management, cryptographic solutions and PKI
2.0 Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks
Threat characteristics, threat actors, threat vectors, vulnerability types, indicators of compromise, AI-related risk
3.0 Security Architecture
Architecture models, Zero Trust, data protection, resilience and recovery
4.0 Security Operations
Mitigating controls, asset management, vulnerability management, monitoring, IAM, automation, incident response, digital forensics
5.0 Security Program Management and Oversight
Governance/risk/compliance, third-party risk, audits, security awareness training

implications.title: What that means for how you study
bullets: Domain 4 is more than a quarter of the exam. Security Operations alone covers eight separate sub-objectives — mitigating controls, asset management, vulnerability management, monitoring, IAM, automation, incident response, and forensics. Budget real time for it; this course gives it four full weeks.

This is not a Linux-only or a Windows-only exam — it's platform-agnostic. CompTIA's own hardware/software list names both Windows and Linux OS, and specific tools like Kali Linux. This course's labs run on Linux because that's what this site teaches, but the concepts transfer directly to any platform you'll actually work on.

Governance, risk, and compliance are not filler. Domain 5 is only 14% of the exam by itself, but GRC vocabulary (SLA vs. MOU vs. NDA, qualitative vs. quantitative risk, data controller vs. processor) shows up embedded in scenario questions across every other domain too.

Read every acronym like it's a vocabulary word, not a shortcut. CompTIA publishes a full acronym list alongside the objectives — this exam rewards knowing the difference between similar-sounding controls (HIDS vs. NIDS, RTO vs. RPO, SIEM vs. SOAR) cold.

note.title: Read the objectives yourself — from the source
note.text: CompTIA publishes the full SY0-801 objectives document, and it is the only authoritative statement of what is testable — this course was built directly from it. Bookmark it and re-read it in Week 15: comptia.org — Security+.

homelab.title: Build Your Home Lab
homelab.subtitle: Two virtual machines and a free hypervisor — a target to secure, and a machine to secure it from
body: Security+ labs need two roles: something to protect and something to work from. You don't need a rack of hardware — a laptop with 8 GB of spare RAM and a free hypervisor covers this entire course.

CompTIA's own published hardware/software list for this exam names firewalls, IDS/IPS, SIEM tooling, a vulnerability scanner, packet capture software, and both Windows and Linux systems. This course's home lab covers the realistic subset of that list a self-study candidate can actually build at home, using entirely free tools.

startHere.title: Everything in this lab stays inside the lab
steps: Build both VMs on a host-only or internal network — never bridge them onto your real home network or the internet.

Only scan, attack, or exploit machines you own, on that isolated network. Running these same tools against anything else — a neighbor's Wi-Fi, a work system, a random public IP — is illegal in most jurisdictions, full stop.
Snapshot both machines before you start. You will deliberately misconfigure and break things — that's the entire point.

budgetNote.title: Two machines, one job each
budgetNote.text: secure-target: a plain Linux server you hunt for vulnerabilities on, patch, harden, and monitor. kali-tools: a Kali Linux VM that carries the scanning, packet capture, and analysis tools CompTIA names by name in its official software list. Neither needs more than 2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM.

groups.title: Pick a hypervisor
groups.intro: Any of these will do it — pick the one that matches your hardware.

items.name: Oracle VirtualBox
items.desc: The default choice for this course. Free, cross-platform, host-only networking is one click away — exactly what keeps your lab isolated.

items.name: VMware Workstation Pro
items.desc: Free for personal use under Broadcom. Fusion is the equivalent on Mac.

items.name: UTM
items.desc: The practical option on Apple Silicon, where VirtualBox doesn't run.

groups.title: Build secure-target
groups.intro: The machine you'll patch, harden, misconfigure on purpose, and monitor.

items.name: Rocky Linux 10
items.desc: Free, no account, and ships with firewalld and SELinux enabled by default — both named directly in the exam objectives.

items.name: Ubuntu Server
items.desc: A fine alternative if you're more comfortable with apt — ufw and AppArmor cover the same ground as firewalld/SELinux conceptually.

groups.title: Build kali-tools
groups.intro: A pre-built security toolkit distro — this is the one CompTIA names directly on its software list.

items.name: Kali Linux
items.desc: Ships with nmap, Wireshark, John the Ripper, and dozens of other tools this course's labs use, pre-installed. Download the pre-built VirtualBox/VMware image — don't build one from scratch.

cloud.title: No Machine to Install On? Rent One
cloud.subtitle: A single small cloud instance can stand in for secure-target
body: Security+ explicitly covers cloud, mobile, and hybrid environments — so practicing on a real cloud instance isn't a compromise, it's on the syllabus. If you can't run two local VMs, a single small cloud instance plus Kali running locally covers this course.

items.name: DigitalOcean
items.desc: Simple pricing, a Rocky Linux image in the catalogue, and firewall rules you configure right in the console — good hands-on practice for Domain 3.

items.name: Amazon Web Services
items.desc: Security groups, IAM, CloudTrail logging, and GuardDuty all map directly onto Domain 4 monitoring/IAM objectives. Free tier covers a small instance.

items.name: Google Cloud
items.desc: New accounts get free trial credit that can cover this entire course.

after.title: Before you spend anything
bullets: Set a billing alert on day one. Every provider offers one free.
Lock SSH to your own IP address in the security group/firewall rules before you do anything else — this is itself a Domain 3 lab task.
Destroy the instance when you finish the course. Don't leave a deliberately-misconfigured, deliberately-vulnerable box running longer than you need it.

certs.title: The Certification Ladder
certs.subtitle: Security+ is the on-ramp into cybersecurity — here's where it leads
body: Security+ is widely treated as the industry baseline for security roles, and it's DoD 8140-recognized for privileged access on government contracts. But it's still a generalist, foundational certification. Where you go next depends on which direction you're headed: deeper into security operations and analysis, or sideways into the cloud/Linux/DevOps platforms that security work increasingly runs on top of.

items.name: CompTIA Security+
items.why: The certification this course is built around, and the one most job postings that say "security+ required" mean by name.

items.name: CompTIA Cybersecurity Analyst
items.why: The direct next rung on CompTIA's own stackable pathway. Goes deep on exactly what Security+ Domain 4 only introduces: SIEM tuning, threat hunting, and incident response at a SOC-analyst level.

items.name: Red Hat Certified System Administrator
items.level: Intermediate · Linux, cloud, and DevOps pathway
items.why: The recommended sideways move if you're heading toward cloud security or DevSecOps rather than a pure SOC role. Security+ Domain 4's SELinux, hardening, and access-control objectives are RHCSA's daily bread — this is where you go to actually get fluent at them, not just recognize them on a multiple-choice question.

items.name: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator
items.why: Same pitch as RHCSA above, but vendor-neutral — worth it if your target employer isn't specifically a Red Hat shop.

items.name: CompTIA PenTest+
items.why: If Week 6's malicious-activity labs were the most interesting part of this course for you, this is the offensive-security equivalent of the CySA+ pathway.

note.title: If you work for a U.S. government contractor: DoD 8140
note.text: DoD Directive 8140 governs cyber workforce qualification across the Department of Defense. Security+ is the long-standing baseline certification named on the majority of federal privileged-access work roles — pairing it with a computing-environment (CE) credential like RHCSA is a common route to a privileged account on a DoD contract. Requirements change; verify current work-role mappings at the DoD Cyber Exchange before planning around them.

coverage.title: Exam Objective Coverage Map
coverage.subtitle: Every domain and every sub-objective from CompTIA's SY0-801 V8 objectives document, mapped to the week that covers it
coverage.intro: CompTIA groups the SY0-801 V8 objectives into 5 domains and 27 numbered sub-objectives. Every one is covered here, built directly from CompTIA's Exam Objectives Document (version 1.4).
columns: What you'll actually be able to do
rows: 1.0 General Security Concepts
1.1 Explain security concepts and controls

Apply defense in depth, CIA, AAA, non-repudiation, Zero Trust, and least privilege; classify a control by category (technical, managerial, physical, operational) and type (preventive, deterring, corrective, detective, compensating, directive)
1.2 Demonstrate the impact of change management on security
Explain a change advisory board's approval process, impact analysis, backout planning, and maintenance windows, and how allow/deny lists and legacy-application dependencies factor into a change
1.3 Explain the importance of appropriate cryptographic solutions
Generate a self-signed certificate and a CSR, distinguish symmetric from asymmetric encryption, explain PKI's chain of trust, and apply salting and hashing correctly
2.0 Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks
2.1 Explain characteristics of threats and vulnerabilities
Score a vulnerability with CVSS, look up a CVE, and explain a threat's likelihood/impact and a vulnerability's life cycle
2.2 Describe common threat actors and motivations
Distinguish a hacktivist from an insider threat from a state-sponsored actor, and match motivation (financial, espionage, ideological) to actor type
2.3 Describe threat vectors and sources
Identify message-based, image-based, browser-based, network-based, supply-chain, and physical threat vectors from a scenario description
2.4 Explain types of vulnerabilities and attack surfaces
Identify unpatched/unsupported/misconfigured systems, hardcoded secrets, zero-days, and shadow IT as attack surface
2.5 Analyze indicators of malicious activity
Recognize malware families, physical/network/social-engineering/credential/application attacks, and read indicators of compromise (hashes, IPs, log manipulation, impossible travel)
2.6 Summarize threats and vulnerabilities associated with AI usage
Explain model poisoning, prompt injection, data loss, hallucination, and jailbreaking as they apply to an organization deploying AI tools
3.0 Security Architecture
3.1 Compare security implications of different architecture models
Contrast cloud deployment models, on-premises, air-gapped, and microservice architectures on availability, resilience, and cost
3.2 Manage the security architecture to protect infrastructure
Apply Zero Trust architecture, secure remote access (VPN, tunneling), and least-privilege identity management to a network design
3.3 Summarize concepts and strategies used to protect data
Classify data (public through top secret), apply masking/hashing/tokenization, and map data protection roles (owner, custodian, steward, controller)
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
Design redundancy (load balancing, clustering, UPS), define RTO/RPO/MTTR/MTBF, and distinguish hot/warm/cold recovery sites
4.0 Security Operations
4.1 Apply mitigating controls, techniques, and solutions
Configure a host firewall and IDS/IPS rule, set up a honeypot concept, and explain DMARC/SPF/DKIM email security and SELinux enforcement
4.2 Explain security implications of hardware/software/data asset management
Walk an asset through its full life cycle — planning, acquisition, assignment, monitoring, and secure decommissioning
4.3 Perform tasks associated with vulnerability management
Run a vulnerability scan, prioritize findings by severity, and write up remediation, verification, and responsible-disclosure reporting
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
Aggregate logs, tail syslog, and explain SIEM, DLP, NetFlow, and SCAP at a working level
4.5 Apply concepts related to identity and access management
Provision and deprovision an account, configure MFA, and apply role-based vs. time-based vs. just-in-time access control
4.6 Apply automation and orchestration to secure operations
Write a script that automates a repetitive security task, and explain guardrails and CI/CD's place in SecOps
4.7 Summarize incident response activities
Walk the full IR lifecycle — preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review — using a tabletop scenario
4.8 Use data, artifacts, and sources to support a security investigation
Preserve a chain of custody, capture a memory dump and bit-level image, and identify which log/data source answers which investigative question
5.0 Security Program Management and Oversight
5.1 Explain the importance of governance, risk, and compliance artifacts
Distinguish a guideline from a standard from a policy from a procedure, and locate a BYOD/AUP/incident-response policy's actual requirements
5.2 Explain the impact of risk management processes
Build a risk register entry, calculate SLE × ARO = ALE, and choose between transferring, accepting, avoiding, and mitigating a risk
5.3 Explain assessment and management of third-party risk
Distinguish an SLA from an MOU from an NDA, and explain vendor due diligence and the right-to-audit clause
5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance
Explain consequences of non-compliance, and apply privacy concepts (right to be forgotten, controller vs. processor)
5.5 Explain concepts associated with audit and assessment activities
Distinguish a known-environment from an unknown-environment penetration test, and place MITRE ATT&CK and the Cyber Kill Chain correctly
5.6 Apply security awareness concepts to improve organizational security
Design a security awareness program's training types, delivery mechanisms, and effectiveness metrics

weeks.title: The 15-Week Plan
weeks.subtitle: Check tasks off as you go — your progress is saved in this browser

items.title: Security Concepts and Controls
items.summary: The vocabulary you'll reuse in every other week: CIA, AAA, Zero Trust, and how to classify any control you'll ever encounter.
tasks: Explain confidentiality, integrity, and availability with a real example of each being violated
Explain authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) as three separate, sequential steps
Apply the principle of least privilege to a sample user account
Classify five real-world controls by category (technical/managerial/physical/operational) and type (preventive/detective/corrective/compensating/deterring/directive)
Explain Zero Trust's "never trust, always verify" principle in one paragraph, from memory
objectives: 1.1 Explain security concepts and controls

items.title: Change Management and Cryptography
items.summary: Two objectives that don't look related until you realize every crypto rollout is itself a change that needs a CAB's sign-off.
tasks: Walk a sample change through a change advisory board's approval process, including backout planning
Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, with one algorithm example each
Generate a private key and a self-signed certificate with openssl
Generate a certificate signing request (CSR) and explain what a CA does with it
Hash a file and explain what salting adds that a plain hash doesn't
Explain a certificate revocation list (CRL) versus OCSP
objectives: 1.2 Demonstrate the impact of change management processes on security
1.3 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

items.title: Threat Characteristics and Threat Actors
items.summary: Who's attacking, why, and how you'd actually know a threat is credible.
tasks: Look up a real CVE and read its CVSS score breakdown
Explain the difference between a threat's likelihood and its impact using a scoring matrix
Match five threat actor types (nation-state, hacktivist, insider, unskilled attacker, organized crime) to their typical motivations
Explain why an "accidental/unintentional" insider is still classified as a threat actor
Describe a threat intelligence feed and what "life cycle" means for a threat
objectives: 2.1 Explain characteristics of threats and vulnerabilities
2.2 Describe common threat actors and motivations

items.title: Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces
items.summary: Every way in — message, image, browser, network, supply chain, physical, and signal-based.
tasks: Identify five message-based and image-based threat vectors from real phishing/QR-code examples
Explain why a supply-chain or managed-service-provider compromise is harder to detect than a direct attack
Set up a basic host firewall rule on secure-target and explain which threat vectors it does and doesn't block
Explain the difference between an access vestibule and a standard door lock as physical controls
Identify Bluetooth, RF, and NFC as signal-based vectors and one realistic attack against each
objectives: 2.3 Describe threat vectors and sources

items.title: Vulnerability Types and AI-Related Risk
items.summary: The gaps attackers walk through — and the newest category CompTIA added: AI-specific threats.
tasks: Run a basic vulnerability scan against secure-target from kali-tools and review the findings
Identify a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOC/TOU) race condition from a code example
Search a public repository for an accidentally committed hardcoded secret (in a safe, sample repo)
Explain model poisoning, prompt injection, and hallucination as distinct AI risks, with one real-world example each
Explain why an LLM's "explainability" gap is itself a listed vulnerability category
objectives: 2.4 Explain types of vulnerabilities and attack surfaces
2.6 Summarize threats and vulnerabilities associated with artificial intelligence (AI) usage

items.title: Indicators of Malicious Activity
items.summary: The biggest single objective in the exam. Malware families, network attacks, social engineering, and how to read an indicator of compromise.
tasks: Capture and read basic packet traffic on kali-tools with tcpdump or Wireshark, on your isolated lab network only
Identify five malware categories (ransomware, trojan, worm, rootkit, fileless malware) and how each persists
Explain the difference between phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing, and quishing with a real (declawed) example of each
Trigger a failed-login lockout on secure-target on purpose, then find the evidence in the logs
Identify hash, IP address, and log-manipulation indicators of compromise from a sample incident log
objectives: 2.5 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

items.title: Architecture Models and Zero Trust
items.summary: How environments are actually built, and how Zero Trust changes the default assumption from "trusted network" to "prove it every time."
tasks: Compare public, private, hybrid, and community cloud deployment models on cost, control, and risk
Explain microservices and logical/physical segmentation as architecture choices, not just buzzwords
Configure a VPN or SSH tunnel between your two lab VMs and explain what it protects
Design a basic Zero Trust access policy for a sample user, covering device health and least-privilege access
Explain a security service edge (SSE) in one sentence you could say in an interview
objectives: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models
3.2 Given a scenario, manage the security architecture to best protect the infrastructure

items.title: Data Protection, Resilience, and Recovery
items.summary: Protecting data at rest, in transit, and in use — then making sure the whole environment survives a bad day.
tasks: Classify five sample data types by CompTIA's classification scale (public through top secret)
Apply masking, hashing, and tokenization to a sample dataset and explain when you'd use each
Map data protection roles: owner, custodian, steward, controller, and subprocessor
Calculate RTO, RPO, MTTR, and MTBF from a sample incident timeline
Design a backup schedule with retention and restoration testing, and explain what "immutable" backup means
objectives: 3.3 Summarize concepts and strategies used to protect data
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

items.title: Mitigating Controls and Asset Management
items.summary: The first Security Operations week — the technical controls you'd actually deploy, and tracking what you own.
tasks: Configure firewalld or ufw rules on secure-target to allow only the services it needs
Set SELinux (or AppArmor) to enforcing mode and resolve one denial you trigger on purpose
Explain DMARC, SPF, and DKIM's role in stopping email spoofing
Set up a basic honeypot concept — a fake service on an unused port — and explain what it's for
Walk a sample asset through its full life cycle: planning, procurement, assignment, tracking, and secure disposal
objectives: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply mitigating controls, techniques, and solutions to secure the environment
4.2 Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management

items.title: Vulnerability Management and Monitoring
items.summary: Finding problems systematically, and building the visibility to catch the next one before it's an incident.
tasks: Run a full vulnerability scan against secure-target, prioritize findings by severity, and write a one-page remediation plan
Aggregate and tail logs from multiple sources on secure-target with journalctl and a central log file
Explain what a SIEM does that a plain log file doesn't
Explain NetFlow, SNMP, and syslog as three different monitoring protocols with different jobs
Write a responsible-disclosure-style report for a vulnerability you found in your own lab
objectives: 4.3 Given a scenario, perform tasks associated with vulnerability management
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools

items.title: Identity, Access Management, and Automation
items.summary: Provisioning accounts correctly, and using scripting to make the boring parts of security repeatable.
tasks: Provision a new user with least-privilege access, then deprovision it cleanly and verify nothing was left behind
Configure multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a sample service using a soft token app
Compare role-based, time-based, and just-in-time access control models with a real scenario for each
Write a short bash script that checks for a common misconfiguration (e.g. a world-writable file) and reports it
Explain what guardrails mean in an automated security workflow, and one way automation can make things worse if it's wrong
objectives: 4.5 Given a scenario, apply concepts related to identity and access management
4.6 Given a scenario, apply automation and orchestration solutions to secure operations

items.title: Incident Response and Digital Forensics
items.summary: The last Security Operations week — what happens after the alert fires, and how you prove what happened afterward.
tasks: Run a tabletop exercise against a written incident scenario, covering preparation through post-incident review
Walk the incident response lifecycle in order: identification, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
Explain chain of custody and why it matters even in an internal-only investigation
Take a memory dump and a bit-level disk image of a lab VM and explain when you'd use each
Identify which data source (access log, NetFlow, packet capture, surveillance footage) answers a specific investigative question
objectives: 4.7 Summarize concepts associated with incident response activities
4.8 Given a scenario, use data, artifacts and sources to support a security investigation

items.title: Governance, Risk, and Third-Party Risk
items.summary: The first GRC week — the paperwork that decides what "secure enough" means for a given organization.
tasks: Distinguish a guideline from a standard from a procedure from a policy, with a real document type for each
Read a sample AUP and BYOD policy and identify three concrete requirements in each
Build a one-row risk register entry: asset, likelihood, impact, owner, current mitigation
Calculate annualized loss expectancy (ALE = SLE × ARO) from a sample scenario
Distinguish an SLA from an MOU from an NDA from an MSA, and pick the right one for three sample vendor scenarios
objectives: 5.1 Explain the importance of governance, risk, and compliance artifacts
5.2 Explain the impact of risk management processes on the security of the organization
5.3 Explain the assessment and management processes associated with third-party risk

items.title: Compliance, Audits, and Security Awareness
items.summary: The last content week — proving you're compliant, testing that you actually are, and teaching everyone else.
tasks: Explain the consequences of non-compliance across reputational, financial, legal, and contractual categories
Explain the difference between a data controller and a data processor, and what "right to be forgotten" requires of each
Distinguish a known-environment from an unknown-environment penetration test
Place MITRE ATT&CK and the Cyber Kill Chain correctly as two different reference models for the same problem
Design a one-page security awareness training outline covering initial, ongoing, and targeted training types
objectives: 5.4 Summarize elements of effective security compliance
5.5 Explain concepts associated with audit and assessment activities
5.6 Given a scenario, apply security awareness concepts to improve organizational security

items.title: Mock Exam, Remediation, and Exam Day
items.summary: A full timed mock exam under real conditions, remediation of everything you missed, and exam-day logistics.
tasks: Sit a full timed practice exam under real conditions — no notes, no lookups
Score yourself by domain and identify your weakest one
Redo that domain's lab guide from memory, untimed
Review the full CompTIA Security+ acronym list until every one is automatic
Confirm your exam-day logistics: ID, testing method, and what you're allowed to bring
objectives: Demonstrate readiness across all five Security+ domains
Identify and remediate weak domains
Understand exam-day requirements

labs.title: Lab Guides
labs.subtitle: One standalone guide per week — real tools, real scenarios, and a short verification step
labs.intro: Each guide is self-contained: what you're doing, the actual commands or scenario, and how to check you got it right. Hands-on steps run only on your own isolated lab VMs — never against a system you don't own.

note.title: Ethics and legality, once, clearly
note.text: Every scanning, exploitation, or attack-simulation step in this course happens on VMs you built, on a network isolated from the internet and from anyone else's systems. Running the same tools against anything else — without explicit written authorization — is illegal in most jurisdictions. This isn't a formality; CompTIA's own candidate agreement and most employers take it exactly that seriously.

note.title: The cheapest way to fail
note.text: Booking the exam before you can pass a full timed mock cleanly. Security+ mixes multiple-choice with genuine performance-based tasks — sitting it unprepared costs you the full exam fee and a month of momentum. Pass a mock first, then book.

examday.title: Exam Day and Staying On Track
examday.subtitle: The habits that get you there, and the checklist for the morning itself

tips.head: Reboot secure-target after every hardening lab.
tips.text: A firewall rule or SELinux policy that only works until the next reboot is a configuration you didn't actually finish.

tips.head: Keep a break/fix log.
tips.text: Every misconfiguration you triggered on purpose and how you found it in the logs. This is your real study guide by Week 15.

tips.head: Live in the acronym list.
tips.text: CompTIA publishes one alongside the objectives. This exam rewards knowing HIDS from NIDS from WIPS cold, not just "an intrusion detection thing."

tips.head: Treat the performance-based questions as real tasks.
tips.text: If a scenario asks you to configure something, you should have typed that exact kind of command in a lab guide already — not be seeing the syntax for the first time.

tips.head: Don't skip the GRC weeks because they're not hands-on.
tips.text: Weeks 13–14 are the ones people cram the night before and then miss five easy points on scenario questions that reuse the same vocabulary in every other domain.

tips.head: Snapshot before every lab.
tips.text: It removes the fear of breaking things, which is the single biggest thing slowing beginners down.

checklist.title: The morning of the exam
bullets: Government-issued photo ID ready — check the name matches your CompTIA account exactly.
Test your machine, camera, and internet against the proctoring requirements the day before, not the morning of.
Clear your desk completely. No notes, no books, no second monitor, no phone.
Read every question fully — performance-based tasks often bury a key constraint in the second sentence.
Flag anything you're unsure of and come back to it — there's no penalty for reviewing.
Last few minutes: revisit any flagged question once, then submit. Second-guessing a confident answer usually costs points, not gains them.

note.title: If you don't pass the first time
note.text: It's a broad exam and plenty of good candidates need two attempts. CompTIA's score report breaks results down by domain — work your weakest domain for two weeks, sit another mock, and book the retake.

story.title: Why I Built This Guide
story.subtitle: A note from Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
story.photoAlt: Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
body: Shea Bennett started his career in Information Technology as a Helpdesk Analyst with no formal training or background in IT. He had no experience when he left the U.S. Navy, where he served as a Hospital Corpsman assigned to a Marine Corps battalion as a Fleet Marine Force (FMF) combat medic. His dream was to become a medical doctor, but the cost of medical education was simply too high — not something the Montgomery GI Bill alone could cover.

While working as a surgical technologist passing instruments at Naval Medical Center San Diego, he met engineers from a healthcare imaging company and asked one of them for help getting into IT. To his surprise, the man helped him land his first real IT job. Shea then spent the next few years training onsite at that company's headquarters in northern New Jersey, flying back and forth from San Diego. He struggled at first — he's a visual learner, and in 2007 the most common way to learn IT was in-person bootcamps or classroom training, neither of which he could afford.

Then he found video-based IT training, and never looked back. Shea is 100% self-taught. He went on to earn a Bachelor's and a Master's degree from National University in San Diego, and trained extensively alongside various government agencies and U.S. government IT contractors — work that put him in the room for exactly the kind of governance, risk, and compliance requirements Domain 5 of this course covers.

Security is where every other course on this site eventually points. RHCSA and LFCS teach you to run the system; Security+ teaches you to defend it. This course exists because that step — from operator to defender — deserves the same real, hands-on treatment as everything else here, not a slide deck of acronyms to memorize the night before.
quote: This was built for that fundi in Kenya, that hustler in Nigeria, the determined in Rwanda or Ethiopia. The hungry surviving in the UAE. The Indonesian or Filipino brother or sister — determined, but never given a chance or guidance.
story.closing: If anything here is wrong, report it and we'll fix it.
